problems.title: The first feasible prefix is skipped
problems.source_location: Corollary 3.1.1, PDF p. 4; Algorithm 1 and Appendix A.2, pp. 22–23; current rdd/algorithms.py, max_sum_partition and rdd_score
claim: Under additive interval scores and allowed lengths, Algorithm 1 is said to find an optimal full partition.
analysis: Take \(N=4\), minimum length \(2\) and maximum length \(4\). All frame features can equal \((1,0)\); a single two-frame prior interval has duration \(1\), so its endpoint feature matches every candidate. With the author scorer’s default mode, \(\alpha=1\) and \(\beta=0\), angular distance is zero and its score is the negative frame count times \(|1-(e-s)|\). Two-frame segments score \(0\), while the four-frame segment scores \(-8\). The loop begins at \(3\), leaving \(D_2=-\infty\), and hence returns \(-8\) rather than the feasible two-segment optimum \(0\). Interpreting the paper’s outside duration as \(e-s\) instead gives the full segment \(-6\), with the same strict contradiction. If the maximum length is \(3\), the valid two-segment solution is still missed. Invalid-edge scores of \(-\infty\) do not restore the omitted feasible state.
result: The listed algorithm and matching author release fail the stated universal optimum guarantee. Standard additive dynamic programming remains valid; no robot success-rate effect is inferred.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.
repair: Start at the shortest feasible prefix, preserve genuinely infeasible states and backtrack a full partition. The corrected standard recurrence is distinct from a new robot experiment.
problems.impact_rationale: The actual printed algorithm misses a better full partition, and can miss the only feasible partition, on a legal four-frame instance. This directly refutes the central optimal-partition guarantee.
problems.existing_correction_status: The latest target arXiv version and freshly retrieved proceedings Algorithm 1 retain the omitted prefix; the current author repository retains the same loop lower bound. The existing standard-recurrence correction is analytic, with no new robot execution or author adoption established.

problems.title: Linear scorer calls do not bound total implementation cost
problems.source_location: Corollary 3.1.1, PDF p. 4; speed discussion, PDF pp. 8–9; Appendix A.2, PDF p. 23.
claim: With bounded segment length, the paper counts linear scoring calls and later describes linear algorithm runtime.
analysis: With allowed lengths \(2\) through \(4\), the release checks all previous breakpoints before discarding illegal lengths. It makes \(N(N+1)/2+N-5=\Theta(N^2)\) length checks but only \(3N-7\) scorer calls. Full-prefix partition copies add further work. The finite Table 14 budget \(44549/386\simeq115.41\,\mathrm s\) is a valid call-count calculation, not a total asymptotic-runtime proof.
result: The call-count result is preserved; an asymptotic linear total-runtime claim needs restricted candidate loops and path storage assumptions. Finite empirical timings are not refuted.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.
repair: Restrict candidate breakpoints to the valid length band and store predecessor links. With declared interval-access and scoring cost \(C_J\), that gives \(O(NW(1+C_J))\) time for width \(W\).
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.
problems.existing_correction_status: The current author function still scans every previous breakpoint before checking lengths and copies full partition prefixes. The bounded scoring-call statement remains valid; no new end-to-end timing was measured.
